title: My True Child in the Faith
subtitle: 1 Timothy 1:1–2
description: Paul, an apostle by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, greets Timothy, his true child in the faith, with grace, mercy, and peace.
paragraphs: The first of the three letters to Paul's coworkers opens with the authority stated in a single phrase: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,” By command is the register of this whole letter. Paul does not present his apostleship as a career or a calling he chose but as an order received, and the God who commands is named with the title this letter will use for him more than any other: our Savior. Christ Jesus carries a title of his own in the greeting, our hope, and hope will prove to be load bearing here: the hope set on the living God in chapter 4, the appearing awaited at the letter's close. Before Paul gives Timothy a single instruction, he has named the command, the Savior, and the hope the instructions stand inside.

The addressee is named with an affection no other letter of Paul's carries: “To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.” True child is a father's phrase, not a colleague's. Readers of this series met Timothy in Acts, the young man from Lystra who joined the mission and stayed, and they have watched his name run through the letters ever since as the trusted man sent where Paul could not go. Here he stands in the harder posting: left behind in Ephesus, a great city and a troubled church, holding a charge while Paul moves on to Macedonia. The greeting's warmth is not decoration. It is the letter's whole method stated in advance, instruction from a father to a son, correction carried inside belonging.

The blessing itself adds a word the church letters do not usually have: grace, mercy, and peace. Grace and peace open most of Paul's letters; mercy stands between them in the letters to his coworkers and in the little farewell letters of this series, Jude's greeting included, and its presence here is worth noticing because this letter will spend its mercy carefully. Paul is about to give his own testimony as a man who was shown mercy, the worst of sinners made an example of perfect patience, and the young worker reading the charge is first covered with the same word: mercy for the man who has to confront false teachers without becoming false himself, mercy for the work of chapter 5's households and chapter 6's rich, mercy from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

What the greeting does not yet do is state the charge, and it is one verse away: as I urged you on my departure to Macedonia. Timothy was not placed in Ephesus by accident or by his own preference. He was urged to stay, by the apostle who calls him his true child, for a specific and unwelcome task, to instruct certain men to stop teaching what they are teaching. The whole letter unfolds from those certain men, and the next episode begins where the warmth meets the work.

title: Stay at Ephesus
subtitle: 1 Timothy 1:3–7
description: The charge of the letter: stay on at Ephesus and instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines, because the goal of all instruction is love from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.
paragraphs: The charge that governs the whole letter arrives in its third verse, and it is a charge about staying: “As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines” Urged, not ordered, from the apostle who calls Timothy his true child, and the task is as unwelcome as it is specific: confront men already teaching, in a church already gathered, and instruct them to stop. Timothy did not choose Ephesus and Ephesus did not choose its crisis. He stays because the mission's map put Paul in Macedonia and him here, and the letter that follows is the staying made workable, everything a young delegate needs to hold a post he did not pick.

What the certain men teach is described first by its flavor: “or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith.” Myths and endless genealogies: story systems and descent lines, material that generates questions faster than it settles any. Paul's contrast is exact. Their teaching promotes speculation; God's work is a stewardship, something managed by faith toward an end. A genealogy can be extended forever and a myth retold forever, and neither one ever has to produce a changed life. That is the attraction Paul is naming, teaching that can run indefinitely because it never has to arrive anywhere.

Against the speculation he sets the destination in one of the letter's tenderest sentences: “The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.” The goal of instruction, all of it, the confrontations included, is love, and love of a specified kind: sourced in a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. The three sources matter as much as the goal. Teaching that produces suspicion and quarrels has failed even when its facts are right, because it has missed the goal the instruction exists to reach. Timothy's confrontation of the teachers will be measured by whether it grows this love, in the church and in Timothy himself.

The teachers themselves are diagnosed in two strokes. “Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk.” Strayed is the word: they did not begin as enemies of the faith but wandered from the heart-conscience-faith path into talk that fills time and changes nothing. “They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert.” The ambition is named before the error: they want to be teachers, and the confidence they project is loudest exactly where their understanding is absent. Paul does not call their material heresy in this paragraph; he calls it empty, misunderstood by its own teachers, and off the road. The next episode takes up the law they mishandle, because Paul is about to insist that the law itself is good, and that the problem is not the law but its use.

title: The Law Is Good
subtitle: 1 Timothy 1:8–11
description: The law is good if one uses it legitimately, enacted not for the righteous but for the lawless, in a list that ends with sound teaching that agrees with the glorious gospel entrusted to Paul.
paragraphs: Paul turns from the teachers to their subject, and his verdict on the law is not the one Timothy's opponents might expect: “Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately.” The law is good. The whole argument sits inside the if: used legitimately, aimed at what it was given to do, the law is on God's side. The false teachers of Ephesus were not rebuked for touching the law but for mishandling it, wanting its authority without its purpose. Everything in this short passage is a definition of that purpose, stated as plainly as Paul ever states it.

The purpose is a negative first: “We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers,” Law is enacted for lawbreakers; that is its address. The list that follows is carried here as Paul gives it, in his order, which any reader of Exodus will feel moving through the commandments in reverse image: violence against parents, murder, and then the list continues into the sins of the body and of trust: “for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching” Slave traders stand in the list beside liars, people-stealing as a law matter, and the list refuses to stay in one category of wrongdoing. It ends by opening: anyone else averse to sound teaching, the catch-all that ties the law's whole purpose back to the classroom where this letter began.

The tie is made explicit in the verse's own tail: the law's legitimate use agrees “that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.” Law and gospel are not rival systems in Paul's handling here; sound teaching is the point where they agree, and the gospel is glorious, from the blessed God, and entrusted, that deposit word again, to Paul himself. The man about to give his testimony is introduced by his trust. He does not wield the law as a weapon against the Ephesian teachers from outside it. He stands under an entrusted gospel that the law, rightly used, serves.

That testimony is the next thing in the letter, and its placement is the argument. Having said who the law is for, Paul is about to name himself as its Exhibit A, a man who belonged on its list and was shown mercy instead. The law is good, used legitimately, and its most legitimate use in this letter will be to frame the story of the worst of sinners, told by the sinner himself, one episode from here.

title: The Worst of Sinners
subtitle: 1 Timothy 1:12–17
description: Paul's testimony: formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man, shown mercy, and made the example of Christ's perfect patience under the trustworthy saying, Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst.
paragraphs: Mid-charge, Paul stops to give thanks, and the thanksgiving is his own case file: “I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service.” The apostle commanding Timothy to hold a difficult post introduces his credential, and the credential is not his record. It is that Christ considered him faithful and appointed him anyway, a judgment made about Paul by Another, before Paul's service could argue for it. Strengthened, considered, appointed: the verbs all belong to the Lord, and the man who urges Timothy to stay at Ephesus grounds his own staying power in grace received, not grit possessed.

The record that grace overruled is stated without varnish and at full strength, as this telling carries it: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy.” Three titles from his old life, and each one matches the law's list from the previous episode, the blasphemer among the ungodly, the persecutor among the violent. The mercy has a because clause and it is not innocence: he acted in ignorance and unbelief, and that ignorance is named as the ground of mercy shown, not of wrong excused. Then the measure of it: “And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.” Overflowed is the water word, more than the vessel. The faith and love that chapter 1 set as the goal of all instruction arrived in Paul's own life as flood, not drip.

Then Paul marks a sentence as the church's property, the first of this letter's trustworthy sayings: “This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst.” Worthy of full acceptance: weigh it, receive it whole. The saying itself is the gospel in nine words, and Paul appends himself to it as its largest instance, worst in the present tense, am, not was. He does not graduate from the title. And the reason for his case is given in the next breath, aimed at every reader who will think their own case too far gone: “But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life.” His rescue is a display window. Perfect patience, exhibited in the worst case, as an example, meaning a pattern to measure hope by, for everyone who would believe after him.

Testimony like that cannot end in summary, so Paul ends it in worship: “Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.” The King eternal stands behind the charge and the testimony both, and the Amen closes the letter's first movement. But the letter is not done commanding. When Paul picks the charge back up in the next verse, he will hand it formally to Timothy by name, and he will use the language of war.

title: Fight the Good Fight
subtitle: 1 Timothy 1:18–20
description: The command entrusted to Timothy in keeping with the prophecies about him: fight the good fight, holding faith and a good conscience; and the shipwreck of Hymenaeus and Alexander.
paragraphs: The charge is now handed over in person, father to child, with Timothy's own history attached to it: “Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight,” Entrust is the deposit word again; the same apostle who received the gospel as a trust now passes a command as one. The prophecies about Timothy are mentioned as things Timothy already knows, words spoken over him earlier in his story, and they are given a military use: by them, fight. Good fight is Paul's phrase and it will close this letter's arc in chapter 6; here it opens the commission. Timothy's post is not administration with occasional friction. It is a campaign, and his past words from God are equipment for it.

The fight's equipment is two things held at once: “holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith.” Faith and a good conscience, the pair from the goal of instruction in verse 5, now issued as a soldier's kit. The danger image shifts from the battlefield to the sea: some have rejected the conscience, pushed it away deliberately is the force of it, and thereby shipwrecked their faith. A shipwreck is not a slow drift but a wreck on something hard, the faith in pieces on the rocks, and Paul assigns the cause precisely: the conscience was rejected first, and the faith broke after. It is the letter's psychology of apostasy in a single clause, and Timothy is armed against it by being told to hold both.

Then, for the only time in the letter's opening, names: “Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme.” The telling carries Paul's sentence as written, with its stated purpose kept and nothing built around it: handed over, to be taught, not to blaspheme. Hymenaeus will appear again in the second letter to Timothy with his teaching spreading like gangrene; Alexander is a name Paul uses elsewhere with grievances attached, and this telling merges no Alexanders and invents no biographies. What stands here is the apostle's grief and severity in one act, two men who shipwrecked, handed over in the hope embedded in the purpose clause, that the handing over teaches what the instruction could not.

The opening movement of the letter is now complete: the stay, the law, the testimony, the charge. Paul has shown Timothy the teachers, the tool, the example, and the stakes. Next the letter turns from the fight to the congregation's ordinary life, and its first word for that life is the last thing a war metaphor would predict: first of all, prayer, for everyone, including kings.

title: Prayers for Everyone
subtitle: 1 Timothy 2:1–7
description: First of all, prayer: petitions for everyone, for kings and all in authority, before God our Savior who wants everyone to be saved, through the one mediator who gave himself as a ransom for all.
paragraphs: The church's public life begins, in Paul's ordering, with prayer, and with its width: “First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone” and then, after the sentence's own break, “for kings and all those in authority” First of all is the priority claim: before officers, before households, before the fights of chapter 1 resume, the congregation prays. Four words for prayer are stacked, petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving, as if one verb could not hold the whole practice, and the range is everyone, with the rulers named specifically inside the everyone. In a letter written under empire, praying for kings is not a courtesy; it is doctrine with consequences.

The purpose of the praying is a kind of life: “so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity.” The church asks for conditions in which quiet lives are possible, and the quiet aimed at is not retreat but room: godliness and dignity practiced without sirens. And the praying is anchored in God's own pleasure: “This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,” “who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” The width of the prayer matches the width of God's desire as Paul states it: everyone prayed for because everyone is wanted, salvation and knowledge of the truth paired as the two halves of the wanting. The telling carries the sentence as written, whole, and builds no system on it in either direction; it is the ground Paul gives for the practice, and the practice is the point here.

The ground goes deeper, into the shape of reality itself: “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,” One God, one mediator: the prayer's everyone stands on monotheism, and its access stands on one man. “who gave Himself as a ransom for all” and then, after the sentence's break, “the testimony that was given at just the right time.” Ransom for all matches the everyone of the prayer and the wanting of the Savior; the mediator is not a clerk passing requests but a man who paid. The testimony phrase dates it: given at just the right time, the ransom as evidence presented on schedule, God's timing, not the church's urgency.

Paul's own role closes the passage, stated with unusual insistence: “For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything.” The double oath about his truthfulness suggests the claim was contested at Ephesus, the Gentile mission itself under question there, and Paul answers it the way he answers everything in this letter, by stating his appointment plainly and moving on. The congregation that prays for everyone is served by an apostle appointed to the nations; the width is the man's as well as the message's. Next the letter turns from whom the church prays for to how the church itself gathers, the men praying, the women learning, and some of the most argued sentences Paul ever wrote.

title: Holy Hands and Quiet Learning
subtitle: 1 Timothy 2:8–15
description: The gathered church: men praying with holy hands without anger, women adorned with good deeds, the quiet-learning instruction with its Genesis grounds and its closing sentence, carried whole as written.
paragraphs: The gathered church is addressed first through its men, and the instruction is about the posture of prayer: “Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension.” Everywhere ties the wish to every congregation Timothy influences, and the raised hands, the ancient prayer posture, carry one condition twice over: holy hands, and no anger or dissension. Prayer with dirty hands or a quarreling heart is the contradiction Paul closes off; the fight of this letter is against false teaching, not inside the praying body. The men are not told what to pray here, since the previous passage settled that, everyone. They are told what to set down first.

Then the women, and first their adornment: “Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes,” “but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.” The contrast is between two kinds of display: costly arrangement and costly action. Adorn keeps its place in the sentence; Paul does not say women should not adorn themselves, he says what the adornment is, respectable apparel, modesty, self-control, and then, positively, good deeds, the wardrobe of women who profess to worship God. The telling carries the passage whole and in its setting, and the argument Paul builds from it is carried the same way, as written, in the verses that follow.

The learning instruction comes with its own ground attached: “A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness.” “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” Learn stands first in the passage and it is a command, not a concession: women are to learn, in the quietness Paul requires of learners, and the verse 12 instruction is carried here exactly as written, at full strength, with no softening and no addition. The telling records the instruction as Paul's, in Timothy's Ephesus, and argues neither for its extension nor its limitation; application to other rooms and other ages is a debate readers have carried on for centuries and it is not settled in this retelling in either direction.

Paul grounds the instruction in Genesis as he reads it: “For Adam was formed first, and then Eve.” “And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression.” Formed first is an order argument, and the deception sentence is carried as Paul states it, his reading of the garden account told in Genesis in this series, where readers can weigh the seam for themselves. Then the passage closes with its most debated sentence, carried as written with no explanation invented for it: “Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.” Saved through childbearing has puzzled the church since it was written; translations and teachers have read it several ways, and this telling adds none of them, only the sentence's own condition, continuance in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control, the same four qualities this letter keeps assigning to everyone it instructs.

The passage ends and the letter moves without pausing to officers: if the gathered church prays and learns this way, who should lead it? The next episode opens the overseers' list, and it begins, surprisingly, with aspiration.

title: Overseers in God's Household
subtitle: 1 Timothy 3:1–7
description: The overseer list: a noble task for the man above reproach, husband of but one wife, hospitable and able to teach, proven in his own household, no recent convert, well regarded by outsiders.
paragraphs: The officers' qualifications begin with an encouragement to want the job: “This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task.” Another of the letter's marked sayings, and its content is warmth toward ambition rightly aimed: aspires and desires are both reaching words, and the verdict on the reaching is noble. Overseer is the letter's word for the congregation's shepherd-leader, the office Paul and Barnabas appointed in the young churches of Acts, and the list that follows is almost entirely character. Timothy is not told to find the most gifted men in Ephesus. He is told what kind of men the office requires, quality by quality.

The character list is carried as Paul gives it: “An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,” “not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money.” Above reproach heads the list as the summary, nothing in the life that hands accusers a handle, and the qualities that follow unpack it: one-woman faithfulness stated as the husband of but one wife, carried here as written; steadiness of appetite and temper; hospitality as an office requirement, the door open; ability to teach, the list's one skill, tied to the letter's war over teaching; and a cluster of negatives around wine, violence, and money that read like the false teachers photographed from the other side. The overseer is what the certain men of chapter 1 are not.

One qualification gets its own reasoning, the household: “An overseer must manage his own household well and keep his children under control, with complete dignity.” “For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?” The home is the proving ground, not a private irrelevance: management and care are the same work at two scales, and a man failing at the small scale is not promoted to the large one on the strength of his gifts. Complete dignity guards the method; children controlled by fear or laxity both fail the wording. The church of God phrase raises the stakes of the question, the congregation as God's own household, which chapter 3 will name outright two episodes from here.

Two final guards face opposite directions. “He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil.” Time is a qualification; newness plus office swells into conceit, and conceit's condemnation is the devil's own, pride named as the original fall's pattern. And outward: “Furthermore, he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil.” The outsiders' verdict counts. An overseer's standing with people who owe the church nothing is treated as evidence, because disgrace in their eyes is a snare with the devil setting it. The list ends there, seven verses, almost no duties named and nearly all being. The deacons come next, and their standard rhymes.

title: Deacons, Tested First
subtitle: 1 Timothy 3:8–13
description: Deacons likewise: dignified, not double-tongued, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, tested first and then serving; the women of verse 11; and the standing earned by serving well.
paragraphs: The second office opens with likewise, and the rhyme is deliberate: “Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money.” Deacons are the congregation's servants, the office whose name is the ordinary word for serving at tables and tasks, and their list begins with dignity and runs straight to speech and appetite: not double-tongued, saying one thing to one face and another to the next; not given to much wine; not greedy for money. The servant who handles the church's goods and errands touches everyone's trust daily, and the qualifications protect exactly that surface. What he holds inside matches: “They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.” Mystery of the faith is Paul's phrase for the gospel as a held thing, and the conscience is the same instrument Timothy himself was told to hold in chapter 1; the deacon's inner grip and the apostle's pair, faith and conscience, are one discipline at two ranks.

The deacons' distinctive rule is time: “Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons.” First be tested, then serve: no instant appointments, even for the serving office. Proven-ness is the gate, the same instinct as the overseer's not-a-recent-convert rule, and it will echo again in chapter 5's warning against hasty laying on of hands. This letter does not trust speed in putting people into roles. Character is what time reveals, so time is built into the process as a requirement, not a delay.

Between the testing rule and the household line stands a verse the telling carries as written: “In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things.” The women here have been read by the church two ways, as the deacons' wives and as women serving as deacons themselves, and the sentence is placed inside the deacons' section without a label settling the question; the telling records the verse, notes the two readings have both been held, and takes neither side in the narration. What is not debated in the verse is its standard, which is the deacons' own standard in feminine form: dignity, bridled speech, temperance, faithfulness in all things.

The close returns to the household and then lifts the office's honor: “A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household.” “For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.” Served well earns two things money cannot buy in this letter's economy: standing, and great confidence, boldness, in the faith. The serving office, tested first and proven at home, turns out to be a road to assurance rather than a lower shelf. With both offices described, Paul next explains why a letter carries all this at all, and answers with the letter's center: what the church is, and the great confession it guards.

title: The Mystery of Godliness Is Great
subtitle: 1 Timothy 3:14–16
description: The letter's hinge: how each one must conduct himself in God's household, the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth; and the six-line confession of the mystery of godliness.
paragraphs: Why write a letter full of instructions to a man who already knows the work? Paul answers in the letter's hinge, and he answers personally: “Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things” “in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.” Hope to come soon, write in case delayed: the whole book exists because of a travel uncertainty, apostolic contingency planning preserved as Scripture. And its subject is conduct, how each one must behave, inside an identity stated in three strokes: God's household, the family-house where the officers and widows and slaves of the surrounding chapters are all members; the church of the living God, assembly language for a God who is alive; and the pillar and foundation of the truth, architecture words, the congregation as the structure that holds truth up and holds it fast in a city.

Then the letter quotes what the church confesses, and the telling carries it whole as the common confession Paul says it is: “By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.” Six lines, and they run the whole arc: earth to heaven and back out to the world. Appeared in the flesh, the incarnation stated flatly; vindicated by the Spirit, the resurrection as God's verdict; seen by angels, witnessed in the unseen realm; proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, the mission's two halves, preaching and faith; taken up in glory, the ascension as the final note. It reads like a hymn the Ephesian church already sang, which is the force of common confession: this is not Paul teaching Timothy something new but Paul anchoring the conduct chapters in the creed they already share.

Mystery of godliness is the phrase to hold. Mystery in Paul's letters is not a puzzle but a kept secret now disclosed, and godliness, this letter's favorite word for practical religion, turns out to have a biography at its center: godliness is great because he appeared. The instructions about prayer and apparel and officers are not the church's substance; they are its conduct, and the substance is a person confessed in six lines. That ordering explains the letter's architecture. Everything before this hinge flows toward the confession; everything after it flows from the confession into the later-times warning, Timothy's own discipline, the households of chapter 5, and the money teaching of chapter 6.

So the pillar stands in the middle of the book holding up both halves, and Paul immediately turns it toward danger. The same Spirit who vindicated Christ has something explicit to say about the times ahead, and it is not reassurance. Some will abandon the faith, the next episode begins, and the weapons against it will be thanksgiving, training, and a young man's watched life.

title: The Spirit Says Some Will Fall Away
subtitle: 1 Timothy 4:1–10
description: The Spirit expressly states some will abandon the faith for prohibitions and myths; against them, creation received with thanksgiving, training for godliness, and hope set on the living God.
paragraphs: The warning opens with a source stated as flatly as the confession: “Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons,” Expressly: not a rumor, a statement. Later times carries no timetable in the telling; it is the age Paul's readers live in, and its mark is abandonment with an address, faith traded for deceitful spirits and demonic teachings. The human channel gets a named mechanism: “influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron.” Seared consciences, the instrument of chapter 1 cauterized past feeling, owned by hypocritical liars who perform a stricter holiness than God's own. The strictness is the tell, and its content comes next.

The teaching to come is prohibition: “They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.” Marriage and food, two created goods, refused in God's name. Paul's answer runs on creation and gratitude: “For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected,” “because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” Every creation of God is good is the counter-creed, and the sanctifying agents are not rituals of avoidance but the word of God and prayer wrapped in thanksgiving. Received with thanksgiving should be rejected by no one; the sentence turns the abstainers' own reverence against their rule. Where chapter 2 grounded conduct in creation's order, this passage grounds freedom in creation's goodness, and both stand.

Timothy's counter-move is teaching, not panic: “By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed.” Good servant answers the overseers' and deacons' standards at the delegate's own rank, and nourished makes the teacher a fed man first, living on the words he serves. Then the training program: “But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness.” “For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come.” Myths again, chapter 1's word, refused; training instead, the athlete's discipline turned on godliness, which outvalues bodily training the way both lives outvalue one: promise for the present life and the one to come. Timothy's body is not despised in this letter; it is outbid.

The passage closes on another marked saying and the hope beneath the labor: “This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance.” “To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.” Labor and strive are the fight of chapter 1 in work clothes, and their engine is hope set on the living God, the household God's own title from the hinge verse. Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe is carried as written, the same width as chapter 2's prayer and wanting, and the telling builds no system on the pairing. What it builds is a young man's orders, and the letter now turns directly on Timothy himself: his youth, his gift, his watched life.

title: Let No One Despise Your Youth
subtitle: 1 Timothy 4:11–16
description: Timothy's own orders: command and teach, let no one despise your youth, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, do not neglect your gift, and pay close attention to your life and your teaching.
paragraphs: The orders now come addressed to the man himself, and the first two are the letter's whole teaching method in brief: “Command and teach these things.” Command and teach, authority and explanation together, neither alone. Then the sentence this episode is named for, aimed at the obvious objection to a young delegate giving orders in an older church: “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” The answer to despised youth is not seniority claimed but example set, in five fields that between them cover the whole visible life: speech, conduct, love, faith, purity. Youth cannot be argued away; it can be outlived in public, quality by quality, until the example does what age could not.

Until Paul arrives, one public practice heads the list: “Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching.” Public reading first: the Scriptures read aloud to the gathered church, then exhortation, the pressing of what was read into the hearers' week, then teaching, the explaining of it. The pattern is old, the synagogue and Ezra's platform behind it, and Paul puts it at the center of the young man's interim work. A church fed by read Scripture is harder to feed myths; chapter 4's whole strategy lives in this verse.

Then the gift, and the warning against its quiet burial: “Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders.” The gift came with prophecy and with hands, the elders of the church laid on together, the same previous prophecies that armed Timothy's fight in chapter 1, and the danger Paul names is not rebellion but neglect, the slow unuse of a given thing. Diligence is prescribed as the alternative lifestyle: “Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all.” Absorbed is the total word, in them entirely, and the promised result is visibility, progress evident to all, the example of verse 12 now given its method and its timeline.

The passage closes with the highest stakes Paul assigns to any minister's habits: “Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you.” Life and teaching, watched in that order, persevered in as a pair, and the outcome stated without hedging: salvation, his own and his hearers', riding on the paying attention. The telling carries the sentence as the letter's own claim, the young man's self-watch as an instrument of other people's rescue. It is a severe kindness, and it ends the chapter. Next the letter walks into the congregation's households, older men and younger, widows above all, where the same attention will be applied to everyone Timothy serves.

title: Widows Who Are Truly Widows
subtitle: 1 Timothy 5:1–16
description: The household of God sorted with care: elders appealed to as family, and the widows, family responsibility first, the enrollment of the truly widows, and the younger-widow counsel given with its reasons.
paragraphs: Chapter 5 opens with the manner before the matter, how a young man corrects a congregation of his elders: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers,” “older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.” Appeal, not rebuke, for the older; family words for every age; and absolute purity guarding the younger-sisters line, the young leader's own conduct folded into the instruction. Timothy is being taught to run God's household as a household, where the correction carries the relationship inside it.

Then the letter's longest single topic, the widows, and it begins with honor and a category: “Honor the widows who are truly widows.” Truly widows is the passage's sorting phrase, widows in fact and not only in name, and the first duty assigned is not the church's: “But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.” Family first, as godliness practiced at home and as repayment, the generations owing care backward. The truly alone widow is drawn in one portrait: “The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.” Against her stands the opposite: “But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive.” And the passage's hardest sentence lands on the neglectful family, carried at full strength as written: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” Denied the faith by conduct, whatever the confession says; the letter that began with the goal of instruction as love measures denial in unpaid household duty.

The church's own list, the enrollment, gets criteria: “A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, faithful to her husband,” “and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work.” Sixty years, one man's wife in the mirrored phrase of the officers' lists, and a reputation made of deeds: children raised, strangers housed, saints' feet washed, afflicted relieved. The enrolled widow is not merely a recipient; her record is a ministry biography, and the church's support answers a life of service with service.

The younger widows are refused the list, with Paul's reasons stated as plainly as he gives them: “But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry,” “and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith.” Idleness follows in his telling: “At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention.” His counsel is the practical opposite: “So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander.” And the grief under the policy is named in one clause: “For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.” The passage closes with its burden principle, aimed at the church's capacity: “If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need.” Care is rationed by truth, not by coldness, so that the truly alone are truly reached. Next, the elders who lead this household, and their own double edge: honor and exposure.

title: Double Honor for Elders
subtitle: 1 Timothy 5:17–25
description: Double honor for elders who lead well, protected accusations, public rebuke for persistent sin, the solemn impartiality charge, no hasty hands, a little wine for a sick stomach, and records that surface late.
paragraphs: The elders who lead the household get the widows' word, honor, doubled: “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” Double honor, for leading well and doubly for the laboring preachers and teachers, and Paul grounds the duty in two quoted sayings he calls Scripture, carried here as he cites them: For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.” An ox-law from Deuteronomy and a saying of Jesus stand side by side under one heading, Scripture, and their shared point is support: the worker fed by the work. The church that sorts its widows' support so carefully is told to be at least as careful with its teachers.

Honor carries its guard: “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” The same evidentiary standard the law gave Israel protects the office from the whisper campaign, and it is stated as a refusal first, do not entertain, the unproven charge not even admitted to the room. But proven persistence flips the direction entirely: “But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.” Private protection for the accused, public rebuke for the persistently guilty, the rest of the body taught by the sight of it. Both halves belong to the honor; a church that only protects, or only exposes, has kept half the passage.

The administration of all this is sworn: “I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.” Before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels is courtroom language, the unseen witnesses named as the audience of Timothy's fairness, and its content is impartiality, the hardest discipline for a young man judging his own elders. The next warning shares the same root: “Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.” Hasty ordination makes the ordainer a shareholder in the appointee's later sins; slowness is purity's strategy, chapter 3's tested-first rule now given its theological weight.

Then, parenthetically and personally, the letter's most human sentence: “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” It sits between purity and judgment with no transition, the apostle tending his child's stomach in the middle of church order, and the telling carries it plainly as what it is, personal health counsel to a frequently ill man, neither a rule for the church nor an embarrassment to explain away. The passage then closes with the principle that governs all its sorting, of widows, elders, and candidates alike: “The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later.” “In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.” Some records arrive early and some late, for sin and for good alike, which is why this letter keeps prescribing time: test first, do not be hasty, let the hidden surface. The final chapter turns to the last household relation and the letter's last enemy, slaves and masters, and then money itself.

title: Godliness with Contentment
subtitle: 1 Timothy 6:1–10
description: Slaves and masters as written, the false teacher's final portrait with godliness made a means of gain, and the answer: godliness with contentment, and the love of money as the root of all kinds of evil.
paragraphs: The household code ends with its hardest relation, carried here as written and in its setting, as this series has carried it in Philemon and Colossians: “All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” The stated aim is witness, God's name and the teaching protected from discredit in a world watching the households. And the believing-master case is turned toward more service, not less: “Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles.” Brotherhood is not used as a lever against duty in this passage; it is used as a reason for devotion. The telling records the instruction as Paul gives it to Timothy's church and builds no application on it in either direction.

Then the letter's last portrait of the false teacher, drawn for recognition: “If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching,” “he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions,” “and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of gain.” Conceit with ignorance, appetite for controversy, a harvest of envy and friction, and the root at last exposed: godliness as a means of gain, religion monetized. Means of gain is the diagnosis the whole money passage will answer, and it reaches back to chapter 1's empty talk with the motive now filled in.

The answer is one of the letter's most quoted sentences, and it concedes the teachers' premise before correcting it: “Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain.” Gain exists; it is godliness with contentment, not godliness alone in these men's accounting. The arithmetic follows: “For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it.” “But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.” Nothing in, nothing out, and in between, food and clothing as the stated sufficiency, a definition of enough set deliberately low. Contentment here is not temperament but doctrine, the traveler's inventory applied to a settled life.

The trap on the other road is drawn with the desire, not the possession, as the snare: “Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction.” Want to be rich is the falling point; the plunge is ruin and destruction at the end of foolish and harmful desires. Then the famous sentence, carried in its exact words: “For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.” The love, not the money; the root of all kinds of evil, kinds included as Paul wrote them, not the shortened form the sentence is usually quoted in. And the damage is self-inflicted at the end, pierced themselves, wanderers from the faith with sorrows of their own manufacture. The passage hands the letter to its climax in a direct address, and the next episode opens with two words aimed at Timothy alone: but you.

title: Fight the Good Fight of the Faith
subtitle: 1 Timothy 6:11–16
description: But you, O man of God: flee and pursue, fight the good fight of the faith, keep the commandment until the appearing, beside Christ's confession before Pilate, under the King of kings who dwells in unapproachable light.
paragraphs: Against the whole money passage stands one man addressed by a title used nowhere else in Paul's letters: “But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.” Man of God is Moses' title and the prophets' title in the older Scriptures, and Paul lays it on his young delegate here, at the fleeing point. Flee and pursue run as a pair, away from the craving and toward six qualities that read like the overseers' list turned personal: righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, gentleness. The fight that follows is fought mostly by direction, what a man runs from and what he runs toward, and Timothy is aimed before he is armed.

The commission of chapter 1 now returns at full volume: “Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses.” The good fight, first given with the prophecies, is now given with a grip: take hold of the eternal life, as if the life were present to be seized and not only future to be awaited. And Timothy's own good confession is recalled, made before many witnesses, his public stand at his calling. Paul sets that memory under the order as its fuel; the man who once confessed well in public is told to keep fighting on the strength of it.

Then Paul doubles the charge with the most solemn framing in the letter: “I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate:” “Keep this commandment without stain or reproach until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Timothy's confession before witnesses is set beside Christ's confession before Pilate, exactly as Paul sets them, the delegate's stand and the Lord's stand in one sentence, and the keeping is dated to the appearance, without stain or reproach until then. No timetable is given for the appearance, here or anywhere in this telling; the charge is endurance measured by an event whose timing belongs to God.

Whose timing, Paul specifies, with the letter's final doxology rising out of the grammar: “which the blessed and only Sovereign One” “the King of kings and Lord of lords” “will bring about in His own time.” Carried as the sentence's own shape gives it, the titles land in a heap between the promise and its fulfillment: the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords superlatives the empire used for its own, claimed here for God. And the close of the praise is on his unseeability: “He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.” Alone immortal, a claim this series has heard in the King eternal doxology of chapter 1, now expanded into light no one approaches and an Amen that lands like a seal. The letter has two doxologies, and both of them interrupt charges; Paul cannot command for long before he worships. What remains is one audience unaddressed, the rich, and one object to guard.

title: Guard What Has Been Entrusted
subtitle: 1 Timothy 6:17–21
description: The rich instructed to be rich in good works and take hold of that which is truly life; and the close: guard what has been entrusted to you. Grace be with you all.
paragraphs: One class in the church has not yet been instructed directly, and the letter saves it for the end: “Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.” Rich in the present age is the careful phrase, wealth indexed to this age only, and its two dangers are conceit and misplaced hope, wealth's uncertainty against God's providing. Richly provides all things for us to enjoy is the sentence's surprise: the God of chapter 4's thanksgiving is no enemy of enjoyment, and the rich are not ordered out of their wealth. They are re-aimed inside it.

The re-aiming is a different richness: “Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share,” “treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.” Rich in good works answers rich in the present age, and treasuring up turns their own banking instinct toward the future that matters, a firm foundation laid with generosity as its deposits. Truly life closes the phrase the way take hold of eternal life opened this chapter's charge; the rich and the delegate are reaching for the same thing by different roads.

Then the letter's last command, and it is the first command restated at the level of the deposit itself: “O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called” knowledge, “which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all.” Guard what has been entrusted: the gospel entrusted to Paul in chapter 1, the command entrusted to Timothy in chapter 1, now the whole faith named as a deposit to be guarded, the keeping charge that ran under Jude's letter surfacing here as a job description. The knowledge whose arguments are to be avoided carries its own warning label in Paul's sentence, so-called, and its professors swerved, the straying word from the letter's first diagnosis completing its circle. Grace be with you all is the final line, plural, as written, a letter to one man ending by blessing the whole church he serves.

So the first pastoral closes where it began, with a stay that became a charge, a charge that became a household, and a household held together by a deposit guarded and a confession sung. Timothy remains at Ephesus in the letter's present tense, holding faith and a good conscience, guarding the deposit. The pastorals continue with a second letter to Timothy himself, the most personal page Paul ever wrote, and it waits at its own outline stop next.
